strengths: Strong empirical results on a challenging closed-loop benchmark: UniDrive-WM surpasses the previous best method (ORION) on Bench2Drive across driving score (79.22 vs 77.74), success rate (56.36 vs 54.62), open-loop L2, collision metrics, and multi-ability results, which supports the central claim that planning-conditioned future image prediction provides useful supervisory signal for planning.

The idea of coupling trajectory planning and future frame generation within a single VLM, with generation conditioned on the predicted trajectory (planning token placed before image tokens), is a sensible and clearly motivated formulation that bridges reasoning, action, and visual generation spaces.

The paper systematically analyzes two decoding paradigms (discrete AR with enlarged codebook/MoVQGAN vs. AR+Diffusion with flow matching) and provides an honest trade-off discussion (token granularity vs. continuous latents, resolution constraints), including supplementary comparisons (Tables 6, 7) showing AR slightly outperforms AR+Diffusion for planning.

Ablations (Table 4) isolating detection head, planning head, and image generation contributions, plus VQA ablation, provide reasonable evidence that the image generation module contributes to both planning and understanding performance.
Comprehensive supplementary material with additional visualizations, multi-ability results, VQA examples, and QT-Former details improves transparency and reproducibility potential.
weaknesses: The contribution is largely incremental relative to its backbone: the perception encoder (QT-Former), LLM, LoRA fine-tuning, planning head, and overall training setup are directly inherited from ORION, and the main addition is a trajectory-conditioned generation head. Gains over ORION, while consistent, are modest (e.g., ~1.5 DS points), and it is unclear how much of the improvement stems from the image generation module versus simply scaling/retuning the training recipe.

The abstract and introduction claim that predicted frames 'iteratively refine trajectory generation' and provide bidirectional gradient flow, but the method as described is a one-pass feedforward design; no inference-time iterative refinement loop or closed-loop use of generated frames is demonstrated, so the actual mechanism reducing to an auxiliary multi-task loss is overclaimed.

Missing key baselines in the planning comparison: FSDrive, the closest related unified vision-planning method (cited and compared only on FID), and other recent generative-planning approaches are absent from Tables 1 and 2, making it hard to isolate the benefit of unified generation over alternative visual-thinking approaches.

FID comparisons in Table 3 mix methods trained on different datasets/resolutions (nuScenes-based world models vs. Bench2Drive CARLA data), which weakens the validity of the 6.4 FID claim; no human/LLM evaluation or downstream usefulness metric of generated frames is provided beyond FID.

Several technical details are under-specified or internally inconsistent: the planner introduces a latent variable z_a but omits KL regularization without analysis; the diffusion branch is described as both a conditional denoising process (Eq. 8) and a deterministic reconstruction; the relationship between h_VLM, planning tokens, and the latent query Q in Eq. 6 is vague; notation for conditional distributions is loose.

The ablation in Table 4 is performed only for the AR architecture, so it is unknown whether the image-generation gain transfers to the AR+Diffusion variant; no ablation of the CLIP loss, flow-matching loss weights, or generation resolution on planning performance is given.

Writing quality needs improvement: typos ('image image generation', incomplete sentence 'The project page is available at', 'Traffic Sign ablility'), duplicated citation indices ('[25, 49, 49]'), and occasional grammatical errors reduce polish and could hamper reader comprehension.

Open-loop evaluation methodology differences (per-timestep vs. averaged L2) are acknowledged but the comparison across methods with different protocols remains imperfect; collision rate is reported as 'Box + Collision' without a clean, standalone collision-rate metric, making the claimed 9.2% collision improvement hard to verify from the tables.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely question—unifying scene understanding, trajectory planning, and future frame generation in a single VLM—and the framing of planning-conditioned future image prediction as a bidirectional coupling between reasoning, action, and generation spaces is coherent and well motivated.

Experimental coverage is reasonably comprehensive for an applied contribution: closed-loop Bench2Drive results (DS/SR/Efficiency/Comfortness), multi-ability results, open-loop planning and detection metrics, FID for generation quality, VQA metrics, and ablations isolating the detection, planning, and image-generation heads.

The ablation (Tab. 4) and VQA ablation (Tab. 7) provide some evidence that future-frame prediction serves as a useful auxiliary supervision signal for planning and scene understanding, which is the paper's central empirical claim.

The comparison of discrete AR versus continuous AR+Diffusion decoding paradigms (main text plus supplementary A.3) is a useful design-space analysis for unified driving world models, including honest reporting that AR outperforms AR+Diffusion on driving metrics despite diffusion's fidelity advantages.
weaknesses: Limited novelty over the primary baseline. The architecture is largely ORION [7] (QT-Former encoder, LoRA-tuned LLM, planning head) augmented with generation heads; the AR pathway (codebook expansion + MoVQGAN) and the AR+Diffusion pathway (learnable query + flow matching) are direct adaptations of established unified-model recipes (Chameleon/Show-o, BLIP3o/Transfusion). The claimed contribution of joint unification in the driving domain is incremental rather than a new algorithmic idea.

The headline gains are modest and presented in a way that inflates them. Closed-loop improvements over ORION are ~1.5 DS and ~1.7 SR; open-loop L2/collision differences are similarly small. Quoting these as '5.9% L2 and 9.2% collision rate improvement' without absolute deltas, variance across seeds, or significance testing overstates the evidence, especially given the noise typical of closed-loop CARLA evaluation.

Technical inconsistencies undermine confidence: Eq. (8) is a duplicate of Eq. (6) with no new content; the paper claims a 'differentiable bridge' and 'gradient flow' between planning and generation but never analyzes or verifies gradient coupling (e.g., whether generation losses actually influence planning beyond simple multi-task regularization); the latent variable z_a is introduced but the KL term is dropped with only anecdotal justification; the diffusion branch is described as sampling-based, yet inference is stated to be deterministic reconstruction, which contradicts the framing.

The ablation table (Tab. 4) is internally inconsistent—rows omit metrics with dashes in ways that make the contributions of individual components hard to verify (e.g., the first row reports L2/collision but no detection metrics; row structure does not cleanly correspond to the described configurations), and the supplementary AR vs. AR+Diffusion comparison (Tab. 6) is not reconciled with the main-text claim that AR+Diffusion yields 'superior performance on visually complex scenes.'

Evaluation details are thin: the FID comparison to FSDrive and other world models (Tab. 3) is run at low resolution (192×128 / 256×256) on future frames whose conditioning regimes differ across methods, and it is unclear whether FID comparisons are protocol-matched. Only front-view image generation is predicted, which limits the 'world model' claim given multi-view inputs. There is no inference-cost/latency analysis despite real-time claims for the AR branch.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a camera-ready venue: duplicated phrases ('image image generation'), an empty project-page link in the abstract, duplicated reference [49] in the introduction, inconsistent notation (st as state vs. image embedding), and vague formulations of the joint objective weaken the manuscript's polish and reproducibility (no code or training-data details sufficient to reproduce the two-stage pipeline).

strengths: The unified framework combining scene understanding, trajectory planning, and planning-conditioned future frame generation in a single VLM is well-motivated and clearly positioned relative to world-model, unified understanding-generation, and VLA literature.

Empirical results are comprehensive and favorable: the method surpasses ORION on Bench2Drive closed-loop metrics (DS 79.22 vs 77.74, SR 56.36 vs 54.62), improves open-loop L2 and collision metrics (Tab. 2), improves multi-ability scores (Tab. 5), and achieves competitive FID for future frame prediction (6.4/7.1, Tab. 3).

Comparing two decoding paradigms (discrete AR vs. AR+Diffusion with flow matching) within the same framework is a useful design-space analysis, with honest discussion of trade-offs (resolution limits of AR vs. fidelity of diffusion).

Ablations (Tab. 4, Tab. 7) support the claim that image generation supervision provides auxiliary benefits to planning, detection, and VQA, and the supplementary adds VQA visualizations and qualitative generation results.
The paper is generally well organized, with clear formulation (Eqs. 1-2) and a sensible two-stage training strategy.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely architectural integration of existing components: the QT-Former, LLM, LoRA fine-tuning, and training setup follow ORION closely, while the AR codebook-enlargement and flow-matching/AR+Diffusion designs closely mirror Chameleon/Show-o and BLIP3o/Transfusion. The contribution reads as an application/adaptation of unified multimodal models to driving rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Several headline claims are not substantiated by experiments. The abstract and introduction claim the generated frames 'iteratively refine trajectory generation' and enable 'bidirectional coupling—both information flow and gradient flow' and counterfactual/causal reasoning ('what if the pedestrian accelerates?'). No experiment demonstrates iterative refinement of trajectories using generated frames, and the causal-reasoning capability is never tested.

The claimed margin of improvement is modest and stated as percentages of already-small values (5.9% L2, 9.2% collision rate relative). Absolute gains over the ORION baseline are small (e.g., L2 1s: 0.268 vs 0.247; Box+Collision 1s: 0.00213 vs 0.00198), and no variance over multiple runs or statistical significance is reported.

The AR+Diffusion formulation has notation and content issues: Eq. (8) is identical to Eq. (6) and adds nothing; the diffusion convention (X0 noise refined toward X1) is confusingly inverted relative to standard notation; the paper states training is deterministic rather than probabilistic sampling, which weakens the 'world model' claim (no counterfactual or stochastic future simulation is actually exercised).

The FID comparison in Tab. 3 mixes methods trained/evaluated on different datasets (e.g., DriveDreamer, Drive-WM on nuScenes-like data) with results on Bench2Drive; direct cross-method FID comparability is questionable without clarification of evaluation conditions.

Ablation table is incomplete: the first row of Tab. 4 lacks detection metrics entirely, and there is no ablation isolating the contribution of the trajectory-conditioning of image generation versus simply adding an image-generation loss, which is the core mechanistic claim.

Minor but noticeable quality issues: broken project page link ('available at' with no URL), duplicate citation [49,49], typographical errors ('image image generation', 'ablility'), and deferred implementation details (loss weights, training schedule) that are not actually present in the appendix, hurting reproducibility.

The paper lacks a limitations discussion (e.g., compute cost of 8×H200 training, single-dataset evaluation, no real-world data, front-view-only generation despite multi-view inputs), and there is no societal-impact consideration despite the safety-critical domain.

strengths: The paper presents a well-motivated unified framework that couples trajectory planning with trajectory-conditioned future frame generation in a single VLM, directly addressing the text-bottleneck limitation of prior modular VLM driving pipelines.

Experimental coverage is comprehensive: closed-loop Bench2Drive results (DS 79.31, SR 56.42), open-loop planning on both Bench2Drive and nuScenes, future-frame FID on two datasets, DriveLM VQA, and multi-ability closed-loop results in the appendix.

Ablations are informative and support the core design claims: removing image generation degrades planning (Tab. 6), the ordering ablation (Tab. 7) shows planning→generation conditioning beats generation→planning, and VQA improves with the generation module (Tab. 8).

The comparative analysis of the discrete AR vs. AR+Diffusion branches (resolution/token trade-offs, latency, fidelity) is a useful and honest contribution, including reporting inference speeds (2 fps vs. 0.4 fps).
Strong FID improvements over recent driving world models (e.g., 6.6 vs. 9.3 for FSDrive on Bench2Drive) with clear gains in planning over the strong ORION baseline.
weaknesses: Novelty relative to ORION is limited: the QT-Former encoder, latent-variable planner, loss design, and training recipe are all adopted from ORION. The genuine delta is adding generation heads and their conditioning; gains over ORION in closed-loop are modest (DS 79.31 vs. 77.74), and it is hard to fully disentangle how much improvement comes from the generation auxiliary task versus additional training/supervision.

Some headline claims are not fully supported. The abstract cites '7.3% L2 and 10.4% collision rate' improvements, yet nuScenes collision (0.31%) is worse than FSDrive (0.19%) in Tab. 3; the provenance of these percentages is unclear. Claims of 'bidirectional coupling (information flow AND gradient flow)' and 'iteratively refine trajectory generation' are weakened by the frozen detection head and the absence of any iterative refinement experiment.

The trajectory planner drops the KL regularizer from the VAE objective based only on empirical instability, with no analysis of latent collapse or distribution quality of z_a; the 'differentiable bridge' is therefore somewhat under-specified.

The AR+Diffusion description is internally inconsistent: Eq. 8 calls it a conditional denoising process, but the training is a deterministic reconstruction via flow matching on latents with an extra CLIP loss; notation (X0 as noise vs. X1 as ground truth in Eqs. 9-10) conflicts with the surrounding diffusion narrative.

Open-loop nuScenes gains are marginal (Avg. L2 0.29-0.30 vs. ORION 0.34), and all reported results appear to be single-run without variance; given the small margins over ORION, statistical robustness is uncertain.

FID comparisons across methods trained and evaluated on the same data distribution, at differing output resolutions (192×128 AR vs. 512×1024 AR+Diff), are not controlled; the paper does not discuss whether resolution or conditioning drives the FID gap versus competitors.

Citation integrity concerns: several references carry implausible future arXiv identifiers (e.g., arXiv:2603.xxxxx, 2604.04198, 2605.05092, 2606.12396, 2606.26017), which undermines trust in the related-work presentation and must be corrected. The project page URL in the abstract is also empty.

Reproducibility is questionable: no code release is stated, closed-loop deployment details (how the 2 fps/0.4 fps model runs in the CARLA loop) are thin, and hyperparameters are deferred to an appendix that remains partial.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant question: unifying scene understanding, trajectory planning, and future-frame generation within a single VLM-based world model for driving, rather than treating them as disconnected modules.

The comparison of two decoding paradigms for trajectory-conditioned future prediction (discrete AR vs. AR+diffusion/flow-matching) is a useful empirical contribution, with a thoughtful discussion of the resolution/token-length trade-off and deployment implications (Sec. 4.5).

Evaluation coverage is broad: closed-loop and open-loop planning on Bench2Drive, open-loop planning on nuScenes, 3D detection metrics, FID for future-frame generation, and VQA on DriveLM/Chat-B2D (Tabs. 1-5, 8-9).

The paper reports state-of-the-art closed-loop results on Bench2Drive (DS 79.22/79.31, SR 56.36/56.42) and low FID for future-frame prediction, and includes several ablations (generation head, detection head, token ordering, VQA).
The supplementary material provides useful implementation detail on the perception module and trajectory planner that clarifies the pipeline.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work. The perception stack (QT-Former), the latent-variable trajectory planner, and the training losses are all adopted from ORION [12]; the AR generation pathway is standard codebook expansion (Chameleon/Show-o), and the AR+diffusion pathway closely follows existing unified models (Transfusion/BLIP3-o/MetaMorph). The contribution is essentially a domain transfer of existing unified understanding-generation techniques onto ORION, with planning tokens inserted before image tokens. Table 7 (token ordering) is the main architectural insight and its gains are small (L2 0.67 vs 0.64).

The claimed gains are modest and inconsistently characterized. The abstract claims '7.3% in L2 and 10.4% in collision rate over the previous best method,' but on nuScenes (Tab. 3) the collision rate (0.31) is actually worse than FSDrive (0.19), and closed-loop improvements over ORION are marginal (DS +1.5, SR +1.8). The 'previous best' baseline selection appears opportunistic.

The paper's central mechanistic claim—that generated future frames 'iteratively refine trajectory generation' and provide 'information backpropagation' between generation and planning—is not clearly substantiated. Since image tokens come after the planning token, gradients from image losses do flow into the planner during training, but no inference-time iterative refinement or closed-loop use of predicted frames is demonstrated; the benefit shown is merely an auxiliary-training-loss effect (Tab. 6), which the framing oversells.

The AR+Diffusion pathway is described confusingly and possibly inconsistently: Eq. (8) duplicates Eq. (6) without adding information; the text says the decoder 'is trained with a deterministic reconstruction loss rather than probabilistic sampling objectives' while also being a flow-matching objective with latent queries; and the roles of Q*, X1, and the latent feature sequence are muddled. The claimed backpropagation of L_CLIP through the pixel decoder is never spelled out.

Serious reference-quality problems: multiple citations contain impossible arXiv identifiers and dates (e.g., arXiv:2603.26741, arXiv:2604.04198, arXiv:2605.05092, arXiv:2606.12396, arXiv:2606.26017, all dated 2026), and Sec. 1 cites '[35, 66, 66]' with a duplicated reference. This suggests a fabricated or unverified bibliography, undermining confidence in the paper's scholarship and attribution of related work.

The 'world model' framing is overstated: the model predicts a single short-horizon front-view frame (192x128 for AR) conditioned on its own plan; no multi-step rollout, no counterfactual action conditioning at inference (e.g., the 'what if the pedestrian accelerates?' scenario from the introduction is never evaluated), and no demonstration that predicted frames causally reflect the planned action beyond qualitative figures.

Reproducibility concerns: the project-page URL in the abstract is empty, no code release is stated, experiments require 8x H200 GPUs, and several key training details (loss weighting between L_CE, L_plan, L_FM, L_CLIP; codebook expansion size; MoVQGAN details) are not provided even in the appendix.

Comparison fairness for FID (Tab. 4) is questionable: baselines were trained with different data, resolutions, and objectives; the paper's model is trained end-to-end on the same driving datasets as the planners while generative baselines are not, so FID gains may partly reflect easier conditioning rather than better world modeling.

Discrepancies between reported numbers and claims: Table 6 ablation rows are hard to parse (rows without detection head have no perception metrics, and one row lists detection+planning but no image-gen row distinction clearly), and the comfortness metric in Tab. 1 shows a counterintuitive jump for the proposed methods relative to ORION without explanation.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely problem: unifying scene understanding, trajectory planning, and future image generation in a single VLM-based world model, rather than treating these as separate modules with text-only intermediates. The motivation about the information bottleneck of text-based pipelines is convincing.

Comprehensive experimental evidence: the method is evaluated on closed-loop (Bench2Drive DS/SR), open-loop (Bench2Drive and nuScenes L2/collision), future-frame generation (FID on two datasets), VQA (DriveLM GVQA and Chat-B2D), and multi-ability closed-loop tasks (Appendix Tab. 9), showing consistent improvements over strong baselines including ORION, DriveTransformer, and FSDrive.

The dual decoding paradigm analysis (discrete AR vs. AR+Diffusion with flow matching) is a useful contribution, with a clear discussion of resolution/token-length trade-offs and deployment roles. The ordering ablation (Tab. 7, planning-conditioning vs. generation-conditioning) is a thoughtful experiment supporting the claimed causal direction (action -> future observation).

Ablations (Tab. 6, Tab. 8) substantiate the central claim that the image-generation head provides auxiliary supervision that improves planning, perception, and VQA, rather than being a decorative addition.

The paper is generally clearly written, with a well-structured formulation (Eq. 1-2), an explicit training pipeline (two stages), and a substantial appendix covering perception details, planner design, and qualitative results.
weaknesses: The architectural novelty is limited: the perception backbone (QT-Former), planner (latent-variable trajectory decoder), and much of the training recipe are directly adopted from ORION, and the unified understanding-generation paradigm follows recent general-purpose works (Chameleon, Show-o, Transfusion, BLIP3-o, Metamorph). The core contribution is essentially the coupling of planning tokens with a future-image generation head in the driving domain; the paper should more clearly delineate its technical novelty beyond ORION + generation head.

The headline claim of 'iteratively refine trajectory generation' and bidirectional information/gradient flow between reasoning, action, and generation (Fig. 1 'Information Backpropagation') is not convincingly demonstrated. It is unclear whether gradients from the image generation losses (L_FM, L_CLIP) actually flow back into and improve the planner, or whether the generation branch is merely an auxiliary task. An experiment isolating gradient flow (e.g., detaching the planner before the generation head) would strengthen this claim.

Closed-loop gains over the ORION baseline are modest (DS 79.31 vs 77.74; SR 56.42 vs 54.62), while nuScenes collision rate (0.31) is actually worse than FSDrive (0.19) and Doe-1 (0.21) in Tab. 3, which is not discussed. The relative improvements (7.3% L2, 10.4% collision) should be stated relative to which baseline and with variance/statistical significance where possible.

Comparison with FSDrive, the most relevant unified vision-planning framework, is limited to FID and brief discussion; a direct planning-metric comparison or explanation of why it is absent would be appropriate.

Several design choices lack justification or analysis: the Gaussian latent z_a is introduced but the KL term is dropped with only an empirical note; the behavior of the latent space without regularization (posterior behavior, diversity of trajectories) is not analyzed. Similarly, the AR branch codebook expansion and MoVQGAN detokenization receive little implementation detail.

Inference speed (2 fps AR, 0.4 fps AR+Diff) raises practicality concerns for the closed-loop driving setting, and it is unclear which branch is actually used during the closed-loop Bench2Drive evaluation.

Reproducibility support is thin in the main text: the project page link is incomplete in the abstract, no code release is stated, and some hyperparameters (loss weights, codebook size, training schedules) are deferred to the appendix. Minor issues include a duplicated citation [35, 66, 66] and occasional typos.

There is no discussion of limitations or societal impact (e.g., failure modes of generated futures, safety implications of generative planning signals), which would be expected for a driving-systems paper at this level.
